extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political philosophy; policymakers and thinkers concerned with liberty and the limits of social authority
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines about when society may legitimately exercise authority over an individual’s conduct versus when individuals must have freedom to develop their faculties and live their own lives. The chapter articulates the harm-principle style boundary and accompanying justifications and warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality as development
rubrics_metrics.description: “Individuality is the same thing with development, and that it is only the cultivation of individuality which produces, or can produce, well-developed human beings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivating each person's unique faculties makes persons more valuable to themselves and to others; human excellence arises from allowing individuals to develop within limits set by others' rights and interests. Anti-pattern: forcing a single mould on all persons (‘wearing down into uniformity all that is individual’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Society may enforce prevention of injury and fair contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is justified in enforcing conduct consisting, first, in not injuring the interests of one another (rights), and secondly, in each person's bearing his share ... of the labours and sacrifices incurred for defending the society or its members from injury and molestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/social coercion is appropriate to prevent direct harm to others and to require equitable sharing of burdens for common defence or protection. These are proper grounds for societal jurisdiction 'at all costs' against those who withhold fulfilment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle / perfect freedom in self-regarding matters
rubrics_metrics.description: “But there is no room for entertaining any such question when a person's conduct affects the interests of no persons besides himself... In all such cases there should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct only concerns the actor (adults of ordinary understanding), society should neither legally nor socially coerce; persuasion and education are permitted but not compulsion. This is presented as a general rule limiting social authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social censure permissible where law is not
rubrics_metrics.description: “The offender may then be justly punished by opinion though not by law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an act is hurtful to others but does not violate constituted rights, society may justifiably respond with condemnation, ostracism, or moral disapproval (opinion) but should refrain from legal punishment. Distinguish social enforcement from legal coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference must be justified by general welfare and evaluated cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: “As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction ... and the question whether the general welfare will or will not be promoted by interfering with it, becomes open to discussion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when conduct affects others, interference should be justified by an assessment of whether it promotes general welfare; there is no automatic warrant for coercion simply because others are affected. Beware misapplying general presumptions to particular cases; they may be wrong or misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom necessary for originality and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: “Genius can only breathe freely in an atmosphere of freedom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality and the introduction of improvements or new practices require an environment that tolerates nonconformity. Society benefits indirectly from permitting eccentric or innovative behaviour, since such persons are often the ‘salt of the earth’ who prevent stagnation. Anti-pattern: flattening society to mediocrity by stifling originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for eccentricity and nonconformity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Precisely because the tyranny of opinion is such as to make eccentricity a reproach, it is desirable, in order to break through that tyranny, that people should be eccentric.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eccentricity should be protected and even encouraged because it serves as a corrective to tyranny of opinion and fosters mental vigour and moral courage. Persecuting or pathologizing eccentricity (e.g., declaring people insane for nonconformity) is cited as a grave social ill and anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and persuasion rather than compulsion for self-regarding virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is equally the business of education to cultivate both [self-regarding and social virtues]... and it is by the former only that, when the period of education is past, the self-regarding virtues should be inculcated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While promoting virtues is appropriate, after education compulsion is not: use conviction, persuasion, exhortation to influence personal conduct rather than coercive measures. Social efforts to improve others should avoid using ‘whips and scourges’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of situations as a condition of development
rubrics_metrics.description: Two necessary conditions of human development are freedom, and variety of situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different persons require different conditions for spiritual and moral growth; social policies that homogenize circumstances (through education, commerce, communication) reduce opportunities for diverse development and thus for overall progress. Preserve a plurality of paths and social variety to sustain improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism of custom inhibits progress
rubrics_metrics.description: “The despotism of custom is everywhere the standing hindrance to human advancement ... The greater part of the world has, properly speaking, no history, because the despotism of Custom is complete.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary conformity that proscribes singularity produces stationariness; modern analogues include mass public opinion and fashions that enforce uniformity. Defense of liberty is presented as the reliable source of improvement because it allows many independent centres of innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality benefits the social whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “In proportion to the development of his individuality, each person becomes more valuable to himself, and is therefore capable of being more valuable to others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing individuals to develop their own natures increases the richness and usefulness of society as a whole: originality preserves and rejuvenates established beliefs/practices, and individuals’ distinct contributions strengthen social ties and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits: society concerned with things that chiefly interest society
rubrics_metrics.description: “To individuality should belong the part of life in which it is chiefly the individual that is interested; to society, the part which chiefly interests society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate domains of autonomy vs. social oversight according to who is primarily affected: personal pursuits belong to the individual, collective concerns to society. This is offered as a principle for delimiting rightful social authority.
